new_statements.quote: 1.15. Khotanese had a stress accent that lay on the first heavy syllable from the end of the word but not on the final syllable itself. A heavy syllable is defined as a syllable containing a long or nasalised vowel or a syllable ending in one or more consonants. Thus, yanīmä /jaˈniːmə/ ‘I do’ (2) is stressed on the penult (second last syllable) because it contains the long vowel ī, while namaśtä /naˈmaštə/ ‘he worships’ (2) is stressed on the penult because it ends in the consonant ś. 1.16. Words containing no heavy syllables or whose only heavy syllable is their final syllable are stressed on the first syllable e.g. pharu /ˈpʰaru/ ‘many’, thato /ˈtʰa’oː/ ‘quickly’, hvatana /ˈhwa’ana/ ‘the Khotanese’.
new_statements.citation: Emmerick, Ronald E. 2024. A Handbook of Khotanese. Completed and edited by Mauro Maggi, John S. Sheldon and Nicholas Sims-Williams (Beitraege zur Iranistik 51). Wiesbaden: Dr. Ludwig Reichert Verlag. doi:10.29091/9783752002898.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Unbounded, quantity-sensitive, right-edge oriented with final-syllable extrametricality: stress the rightmost heavy syllable (long/nasalised vowel or closed) excluding the word-final syllable; if there is no non-final heavy syllable, stress the initial syllable (default-to-opposite-edge). E.g. ya.ˈnī.mä, na.ˈmaś.tä, but ˈpha.ru, ˈtha.to (final heavy ignored), ˈhva.ta.na.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Emmerick's sample says nothing about secondary stress. Sims-Williams (2022 TOC sec. 6.2.5; 2025 IIJ p. 343; 2025a Reader p. 79) posits that many words of more than two syllables carry both a primary and a secondary word-stress, the metrical an earlier reading in 9-/10-mora cadences sometimes falling on the secondary; Hitch 2016: 125 assumes secondary stress on certain verb endings. No positional algorithm for secondary stress is given in any opened text.
new_statements.exceptions: (i) Maggi 1992 (as reported by Sims-Williams 2022: 22) calls the stress only 'quasi-fixed': words of four or more syllables with abl. sg. m. -äna or loc. pl. -uvo' are stressed on the antepenult even when it is light. (ii) Sims-Williams 2025a: 19 rejects the final-syllable exclusion: 'all or most words ending with a syllable containing a long vowel or diphthong are stressed on that syllable' (thaˈtau, hvaˈtai, aysˈmū), contra Emmerick's ˈthato. (iii) Sims-Williams 2025: 343-344: morphologically conditioned contrasts such as HˈHL uysˈnora vs ˈHHL ˈsarbīndä (finite verbs with heavy monosyllabic stem + HL ending keep stem stress) and HˈLL hanˈdara vs ˈHLL ˈsarbätĕ; mobile stress in inflection (2022 TOC sec. 6.2.1). (iv) Konow 1932: 13-14 (older, diachronic) notes tendencies to shift stress to a long antepenult or a verbal prefix and some short stressed penults. All authors agree a final LIGHT syllable of a polysyllable is never stressed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress of (Old) Khotanese, an extinct Middle Iranian language; the Handbook presents an idealised Old Khotanese in normalised orthography with stress-marked phonemic citation forms. The position of stress is reconstructed from orthographic alternations (palatalisation in stressed syllables, weakening/loss of unstressed vowels) and from the metre of the Book of Zambasta, and Sims-Williams (2025a: 19; 2025: 330) explicitly calls Khotanese accentuation 'highly controversial'. Late Khotanese (with heavy vowel loss) is not separately characterised in the opened pages.
new_statements.identity_note: saka1300 'Sakan' [xsk] is a Glottolog Bookkeeping languoid for a retired ISO 639-3 code that duplicated Khotanese [kho] = khot1251 (a sibling check folder already holds the same handbook sample). by our rule that each source is filed under the language's current Glottolog code (a retired code does not make a separate language) this key should MERGE into khot1251, not be counted as a distinct language. The quoted statement describes (idealised) Old Khotanese, the 5th-8th c. language of the Book of Zambasta and other Buddhist texts; the language is extinct and its stress is reconstructed philologically (vowel weakening/palatalisation, metre), not observed. Late Khotanese and the sister Saka language Tumshuqese (tums1237) are not covered by the statement.

sources.note: p. 9 sec. 1.15: stress accent on the first heavy syllable from the end of the word but not on the final syllable; heavy = long or nasalised vowel or closed syllable. sec. 1.16: words with no heavy syllable, or whose only heavy syllable is final, are stressed on the first syllable (pharu, thato, hvatana). All vocabulary in ch. 1-13 is given with stress-marked phonemic transcriptions. TOC shows Part II sec. 4 Phonology pp. 284-288 (not in sample).

sources.note: p. 19: 'my views on the position of the stress in Old Khotanese differ from those of Emmerick.. Emmerick took the view that no word bears a stress on its final syllable (Intro. sec. 1.15), whereas in my view all or most words ending with a syllable containing a long vowel or diphthong are stressed on that syllable' (thaˈtau vs Emmerick's [ˈtʰa'oː]). p. 79: cadence an earlier reading generally coincides with primary word-stress, in 9-/10-mora cadences may fall on a secondary stress. Metrically scanned text pp. 82-102 marks an earlier reading.

sources.note: sec. 6 pp. 342-344: postulates that the final light syllable of a polysyllabic word never bears the stress and that many words of 3+ syllables have primary and secondary stress; HL/LHL words 'stressed on the heavy penultimate syllable (in accordance with the rule stated by Maggi 1992: 52, sec. 80; Emmerick 2024: 9, sec. 1.15)'; contrasts uysˈnora HˈHL vs ˈsarbindä ˈHHL (finite-verb stress rules, S-W 2022: 76-77), hanˈdara HˈLL vs ˈsarbätĕ ˈHLL. Frames the whole question as an ongoing controversy (Fattori 2025, Hitch deny stress a metrical role).

sources.note: 'Stress' pp. 12-15: 'The accent was a stress-accent, and its position depended on length. A long penultima carried the stress.. If the penultima was short, the antepenultima was regularly stressed if it was the first syllable of the word or if it was long', with tendencies to shift to a long antepenult or a prefix; inferred mainly from pre-Khotanese vowel shortening/loss (diachronic), author disclaims an exhaustive account pending metrical study.
